claim: The sense of touch comprises multiple sensory channels that each conveys characteristic signals during interactions with objects.
source: The sense of touch comprises multiple sensory channels that each conveys characteristic signals during interactions with objects.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about the somatosensory system.

claim: The strength of cortical responses is driven by rapidly adapting (RA) nerve fibers.
source: First, we find that the strength of cortical responses is driven by one population of nerve fibers (rapidly adapting) whereas the timing of cortical responses is shaped by the other (Pacinian).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and modeling results presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 3.

claim: The timing of cortical responses is shaped by Pacinian (PC) nerve fibers.
source: First, we find that the strength of cortical responses is driven by one population of nerve fibers (rapidly adapting) whereas the timing of cortical responses is shaped by the other (Pacinian).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and modeling results presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 4.

claim: Input from RA and PC sensory channels is integrated in an optimal fashion that exploits the disparate response behaviors of different fiber types.
source: Second, we show that input from these sensory channels is integrated in an optimal fashion that exploits the disparate response behaviors of different fiber types.
evidence: This claim is supported by the optimization analysis presented in Figure 5 and the corresponding text.

claim: Signals from different cone receptors are integrated to extract color information in vision.
source: The classic example of such integration is color vision, where input from different cone receptors is integrated to extract a specific feature of objects, approximately corresponding to their absorption spectrum (Gegenfurtner, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Signals are combined across different sensory modalities in an optimized manner to extract stimulus information.
source: Signals are also combined across different sensory modalities, and this integration process is often optimized to extract stimulus information (Ernst and Banks, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The sense of touch is mediated by at least three main classes of mechanoreceptive afferents.
source: The sense of touch is mediated by at least three main classes of mechanoreceptive afferents, each of which responds to different aspects of skin deformation (Johnson, 2001): slowly-adapting type I (SA1) afferents are most sensitive at low frequencies (<10 Hz), rapidly adapting (RA) afferents at intermediate frequencies (in the so-called flutter range, from 10 to 50 Hz), and Pacinian (PC) afferents at high-frequencies (peaking in sensitivity at around 250 Hz).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: SA1 afferents are most sensitive at low frequencies (<10 Hz).
source: slowly-adapting type I (SA1) afferents are most sensitive at low frequencies (<10 Hz), rapidly adapting (RA) afferents at intermediate frequencies (in the so-called flutter range, from 10 to 50 Hz), and Pacinian (PC) afferents at high-frequencies (peaking in sensitivity at around 250 Hz).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Johnson, 2001).

claim: RA afferents are most sensitive at intermediate frequencies (10 to 50 Hz).
source: slowly-adapting type I (SA1) afferents are most sensitive at low frequencies (<10 Hz), rapidly adapting (RA) afferents at intermediate frequencies (in the so-called flutter range, from 10 to 50 Hz), and Pacinian (PC) afferents at high-frequencies (peaking in sensitivity at around 250 Hz).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Johnson, 2001).

claim: PC afferents are most sensitive at high frequencies, peaking at around 250 Hz.
source: slowly-adapting type I (SA1) afferents are most sensitive at low frequencies (<10 Hz), rapidly adapting (RA) afferents at intermediate frequencies (in the so-called flutter range, from 10 to 50 Hz), and Pacinian (PC) afferents at high-frequencies (peaking in sensitivity at around 250 Hz).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Johnson, 2001).

claim: The frequency sensitivities of different afferent classes overlap considerably.
source: However, the frequency sensitivities of the different afferent classes overlap considerably (Figure 1A), and natural stimuli typically engage more than one class (Saal and Bensmaia, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1A showing overlapping frequency response ranges and a citation.

claim: Natural stimuli typically engage more than one class of mechanoreceptive afferents.
source: However, the frequency sensitivities of the different afferent classes overlap considerably (Figure 1A), and natural stimuli typically engage more than one class (Saal and Bensmaia, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Information about most tactile events is carried by signals from several afferent classes.
source: Not surprisingly, then, information about most tactile events is carried by signals from several afferent classes (Saal and Bensmaia, 2014; Johansson and Flanagan, 2009; Abraira and Ginty, 2013), and this input is integrated across submodalities even at the first stage of cortical processing, namely primary somatosensory cortex (S1) (Pei et al., 2009; Carter et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Input from different mechanoreceptive afferent classes is integrated in primary somatosensory cortex (S1).
source: Not surprisingly, then, information about most tactile events is carried by signals from several afferent classes (Saal and Bensmaia, 2014; Johansson and Flanagan, 2009; Abraira and Ginty, 2013), and this input is integrated across submodalities even at the first stage of cortical processing, namely primary somatosensory cortex (S1) (Pei et al., 2009; Carter et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: S1 neurons convey information about contacted objects in both the strength and timing of their responses.
source: Importantly, S1 neurons convey information about contacted objects not only in the strength of their responses but also in their timing (Harvey et al., 2013; Zuo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The amplitude of skin oscillations is encoded in the strength of the cortical response.
source: For example, the amplitude of skin oscillations—such as those elicited during the exploration of textured surfaces—is encoded in the strength of the cortical response whereas their frequency is encoded in its timing.
evidence: This is presented as an example of how S1 neurons encode information, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: The frequency of skin oscillations is encoded in the timing of the cortical response.
source: For example, the amplitude of skin oscillations—such as those elicited during the exploration of textured surfaces—is encoded in the strength of the cortical response whereas their frequency is encoded in its timing.
evidence: This is presented as an example of how S1 neurons encode information, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: Recordings were obtained from 18 peripheral tactile afferents (14 RA and 4 PC).
source: We recorded the responses of 18 peripheral tactile afferents (14 RA and 4 PC) and 118 cortical neurons in areas 3b (49) and 1 (69) of S1 to a variety of vibrotactile stimuli, ranging from simple sinusoids to complex bandpass noise with frequencies between 50 and 800 Hz and amplitudes ranging from sub-micrometer to more than 500 µm.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental data collected.

claim: Recordings were obtained from 118 cortical neurons in areas 3b (49) and 1 (69) of S1.
source: We recorded the responses of 18 peripheral tactile afferents (14 RA and 4 PC) and 118 cortical neurons in areas 3b (49) and 1 (69) of S1 to a variety of vibrotactile stimuli, ranging from simple sinusoids to complex bandpass noise with frequencies between 50 and 800 Hz and amplitudes ranging from sub-micrometer to more than 500 µm.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental data collected.

claim: Stimuli ranged from simple sinusoids to complex bandpass noise with frequencies between 50 and 800 Hz.
source: We recorded the responses of 18 peripheral tactile afferents (14 RA and 4 PC) and 118 cortical neurons in areas 3b (49) and 1 (69) of S1 to a variety of vibrotactile stimuli, ranging from simple sinusoids to complex bandpass noise with frequencies between 50 and 800 Hz and amplitudes ranging from sub-micrometer to more than 500 µm.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental stimuli used.

claim: Stimuli amplitudes ranged from sub-micrometer to more than 500 µm.
source: We recorded the responses of 18 peripheral tactile afferents (14 RA and 4 PC) and 118 cortical neurons in areas 3b (49) and 1 (69) of S1 to a variety of vibrotactile stimuli, ranging from simple sinusoids to complex bandpass noise with frequencies between 50 and 800 Hz and amplitudes ranging from sub-micrometer to more than 500 µm.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental stimuli used.

claim: Stimulation conditions spanned those that might be experienced when scanning a textured surface.
source: Stimulation conditions spanned those that might be experienced when we scan a textured surface (Bensmaïa and Hollins, 2003; Bensmaïa and Hollins, 2005; Weber et al., 2013; Manfredi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work characterizing natural texture scanning.

claim: The stimuli used drove RA and PC afferents to the exclusion of SA1 afferents.
source: As these stimuli drove RA and PC to the exclusion of SA1 afferents (Muniak et al., 2007), we focused the analysis on these two afferent populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and the frequency range of stimuli used.

claim: The model captured 67% (± 2% standard error of the mean) of the predictable variance for 1 s bins.
source: Indeed, across neurons, the model captured 67% ( ± 2% standard error of the mean) of the predictable variance (Ramirez et al., 2014) for 1 s bins, and 35% ( ± 2%) for 5 ms bins.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the modeling analysis.

claim: The model captured 35% (± 2% standard error of the mean) of the predictable variance for 5 ms bins.
source: Indeed, across neurons, the model captured 67% ( ± 2% standard error of the mean) of the predictable variance (Ramirez et al., 2014) for 1 s bins, and 35% ( ± 2%) for 5 ms bins.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the modeling analysis.

claim: Most cortical neurons in areas 3b and 1 receive input from both RA and PC afferents.
source: We found that most cortical neurons in areas 3b and 1 receive input from both RA and PC afferents, as evidenced by the significant contribution of both to the overall prediction (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: RA filters were consistently of lower magnitude than PC filters.
source: First, while the magnitude of the PC filters was correlated with that of the RA filters (r = 0.41), PC filters were consistently of lower magnitude (Figure 2C, t(70) = 6.4, p < 0.01, paired t-test), with the RA contribution on average about three times stronger than the PC one.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the filter magnitudes shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The RA contribution to cortical responses is on average about three times stronger than the PC contribution.
source: First, while the magnitude of the PC filters was correlated with that of the RA filters (r = 0.41), PC filters were consistently of lower magnitude (Figure 2C, t(70) = 6.4, p < 0.01, paired t-test), with the RA contribution on average about three times stronger than the PC one.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the filter analysis.

claim: RA filters were much more extended in time (with a mean above 30 ms) than PC filters (with a mean below 20 ms).
source: Second, RA filters were much more extended in time (with a mean above 30 ms) than were PC filters (with a mean below 20 ms) (Figure 2D, t(188) = 9.6, p < 0.01, two-sample t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of filter widths shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The net contribution of RA input to the cortical response was positive.
source: Third, while the net contribution of the RA input to the cortical response was positive, PC input was on average balanced; that is, excitatory and suppressive components of the PC filters were of equal magnitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by the excitation index analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: PC input was on average balanced, with excitatory and suppressive components of equal magnitude.
source: Third, while the net contribution of the RA input to the cortical response was positive, PC input was on average balanced; that is, excitatory and suppressive components of the PC filters were of equal magnitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by the excitation index analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: For about half of cortical neurons, the PC contribution was net suppressive.
source: In fact, for about half of cortical neurons, the PC contribution was net suppressive (Figure 2E); the difference in the net contribution of RA and PC input was significant (t(188) = 16.1, p < 0.01, two-sample t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by the excitation index analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The difference in the net contribution of RA and PC input was significant (t(188) = 16.1, p < 0.01).
source: In fact, for about half of cortical neurons, the PC contribution was net suppressive (Figure 2E); the difference in the net contribution of RA and PC input was significant (t(188) = 16.1, p < 0.01, two-sample t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis.

claim: The firing rates of individual S1 neurons are almost entirely determined by RA input.
source: Indeed, the firing rates of individual S1 neurons are almost entirely determined by RA input as evidenced by the fact that a model based on RA input alone can predict S1 firing rates—averaged over 1 s long periods—almost as well as RA and PC responses combined; this was true for responses to both noise and sinusoids (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the model comparison results shown in Figure 3.

claim: A model based on RA input alone can predict S1 firing rates almost as well as RA and PC responses combined.
source: Indeed, the firing rates of individual S1 neurons are almost entirely determined by RA input as evidenced by the fact that a model based on RA input alone can predict S1 firing rates—averaged over 1 s long periods—almost as well as RA and PC responses combined; this was true for responses to both noise and sinusoids (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the model comparison results shown in Figure 3.

claim: PC input alone cannot account for the observed cortical firing rates.
source: PC input alone, on the other hand, cannot account for the observed cortical firing rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model comparison results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The responses of mechanoreceptive afferents are highly precise and repeatable.
source: We have previously shown that the responses of mechanoreceptive afferents are highly precise and repeatable, and their timing conveys information about the frequency composition of skin vibrations (Mackevicius et al., 2012) and about the identity of textures scanned across the skin (Weber et al., 2013) at resolutions on the order of milliseconds.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: The timing of mechanoreceptive afferent responses conveys information about the frequency composition of skin vibrations at millisecond resolution.
source: We have previously shown that the responses of mechanoreceptive afferents are highly precise and repeatable, and their timing conveys information about the frequency composition of skin vibrations (Mackevicius et al., 2012) and about the identity of textures scanned across the skin (Weber et al., 2013) at resolutions on the order of milliseconds.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The temporal patterning of responses in somatosensory cortex is precise and informative down to a millisecond timescale.
source: Similarly, the temporal patterning of responses in somatosensory cortex is precise and informative down to a millisecond timescale (Harvey et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: When removing the PC contribution from the model, predictions of spike timing in the cortex became less temporally precise.
source: Indeed, when removing the PC contribution from the model, predictions of spike timing in the cortex became less temporally precise (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Only PC input can account for high frequency fluctuations in the cortical responses of many neurons.
source: We found that only PC input can account for high frequency fluctuations in the cortical responses of many neurons, while RA input is sufficient at coarser temporal resolutions for almost all cortical neurons (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal resolution analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: RA input is sufficient at coarser temporal resolutions for almost all cortical neurons.
source: We found that only PC input can account for high frequency fluctuations in the cortical responses of many neurons, while RA input is sufficient at coarser temporal resolutions for almost all cortical neurons (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal resolution analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The more precise the responses of a cortical neuron were, the more of its response variance was explained by PC input.
source: In fact, the more precise the responses of a cortical neuron were, the more of its response variance was explained by PC input (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cortical neurons produce entrained responses to sinusoidal stimulation of the skin over a wide range of frequencies.
source: Second, we tested how well the model could account for the well-documented patterning in cortical responses to sinusoidal vibrations: over a wide range of frequencies, cortical neurons produce entrained responses to sinusoidal stimulation of the skin (Harvey et al., 2013; Salinas et al., 2000; Mountcastle et al., 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The strength of phase-locking to sinusoids ranging in frequency from 50 to 300 Hz was well captured by the model (correlation of 0.78).
source: We found that the strength of phase-locking to sinusoids ranging in frequency from 50 to 300 Hz was well captured by the model (yielding a correlation between predicted and measured phase-locking of 0.78).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model validation.

claim: RA input was dominant at low frequencies for phase-locking.
source: Importantly, while RA input was dominant at the low frequencies, only the PC input could account for the observed phase-locking at 200 Hz and above (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phase-locking analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Only PC input could account for the observed phase-locking at 200 Hz and above.
source: Importantly, while RA input was dominant at the low frequencies, only the PC input could account for the observed phase-locking at 200 Hz and above (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phase-locking analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PC responses to skin vibrations and scanned textures are more temporally precise than RA responses.
source: Specifically, PC responses to skin vibrations and scanned textures have been consistently shown to be more temporally precise than their RA counterparts (Weber et al., 2013; Mackevicius et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PC afferents are considerably more sensitive than RA afferents at frequencies above about 150 Hz.
source: Furthermore, the two afferent classes differ in their frequency sensitivity profile: PC afferents are considerably more sensitive than RA afferents at frequencies above about 150 Hz (see Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1A showing the frequency-amplitude response profiles.

claim: When running a finger across a textured surface, high-frequency oscillations are elicited in the skin.
source: When running our finger across a textured surface, high-frequency oscillations are elicited in the skin (BensmaÏa and Hollins, 2003; 2005; Manfredi et al., 2014), which in turn elicit highly temporally patterned and repeatable responses in both RA and PC afferents (Weber et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Texture-elicited skin oscillations elicit highly temporally patterned and repeatable responses in both RA and PC afferents.
source: When running our finger across a textured surface, high-frequency oscillations are elicited in the skin (BensmaÏa and Hollins, 2003; 2005; Manfredi et al., 2014), which in turn elicit highly temporally patterned and repeatable responses in both RA and PC afferents (Weber et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cortical neurons respond to skin oscillations with precisely timed spikes that encode the skin deflections with millisecond precision.
source: In cortex, neurons respond to skin oscillations with precisely timed spikes that encode the skin deflections with millisecond precision (Harvey et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Most (71%) optimized filters comprised contribution from both RA and PC fibers.
source: First, we found that most (71%) optimized filters comprised contribution from both RA and PC fibers, while the rest relied on RA input alone, similar to what we found in our cortical data set.
evidence: This is a result from the optimization analysis on natural textures.

claim: The optimal filters typically weighted the RA input more strongly than the PC input.
source: Second, we found that the optimal filters typically weighted the RA input more strongly than the PC input, as did the filters derived from cortical responses (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the optimization results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The optimal RA filter widths were wider than PC filter widths.
source: Third, the optimal RA filter widths were wider than PC filter widths and largely overlapped the range of the actual filter widths (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the optimization results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The excitation/suppression indices of the optimized filters approximated those derived from cortical data, with RA input always net excitatory and PC input spanning the range between highly suppressive, balanced, and excitatory.
source: Finally, we found that the excitation/suppression indices of the optimized filters approximated those derived from our cortical data set in that RA input was always net excitatory, while PC input spanned the range between highly suppressive, balanced, and excitatory (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the optimization results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: During natural interaction with surfaces, the amplitude of elicited vibrations decreases as their frequency increases, leading to roughly a power-law relationship.
source: During natural interaction with surfaces, the amplitude of elicited vibrations decreases as their frequency increases, leading to roughly a power–law relationship (Manfredi et al., 2014; Wiertlewski et al., 2011; Delhaye et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When filters were optimized to stimuli with distorted frequency composition, the resulting filters did not match those observed in cortex.
source: When we re-optimized the filters to stimuli with a distorted frequency composition, we found that the resulting filters did not match the ones observed in cortex (green bars in Figure 5B–D): The PC signal was weighted more heavily, was integrated over longer timescales, and was mostly excitatory, in contrast to what we observed in both the cortical filters and the ones optimized on our natural texture data set.
evidence: This claim is supported by the distorted optimization analysis shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: RA and PC integration in S1 is optimized to encode stimuli that are commonly encountered during interactions with objects.
source: We conclude that RA and PC integration in S1 is optimized to encode stimuli that are commonly encountered during interactions with objects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optimization analysis comparing natural and distorted stimuli.

claim: The vast majority of cortical neurons receive (indirect) input from both RA and PC afferents.
source: First, the vast majority of cortical neurons receive (indirect) input from both RA and PC afferents.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: RA input determines the rate of the cortical response whereas the principal contribution of PC input is to sharpen the temporal precision of the response.
source: Second, RA and PC afferents drive S1 neurons in fundamentally different ways: RA input determines the rate of the response whereas the principal contribution of PC input is to sharpen the temporal precision of the response.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the modeling and analysis results.

claim: The integration of afferent input is consistent with a process that maximizes the information conveyed in the cortical responses by exploiting the different response properties of RA and PC afferents.
source: Third, the integration of afferent input is consistent with a process that maximizes the information conveyed in the cortical responses by exploiting the different response properties of RA and PC afferents.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the optimization analysis.

claim: The responses of S1 neurons cannot be explained from the responses of RA or PC neurons alone.
source: Our results unequivocally show that RA and PC input are integrated in the responses of individual S1 neurons. That is, the responses of S1 neurons cannot be explained from the responses of RA or PC neurons alone.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: It has traditionally been assumed that different tactile submodalities are segregated at least through primary somatosensory cortex.
source: While it has traditionally been assumed that the different tactile submodalities are segregated at least through primary somatosensory cortex (Sur et al., 1981; Sur et al., 1984; Chen et al., 2001; Friedman et al., 2004) (although cortical PC neurons have generally proven elusive, see below), recent evidence suggests that input from different classes of somatosensory afferents is indeed integrated between periphery and cortex (Saal and Bensmaia, 2014; Pei et al., 2009; Carter et al., 2014; Prescott et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work representing the traditional view.

claim: Recent evidence suggests that input from different classes of somatosensory afferents is integrated between periphery and cortex.
source: While it has traditionally been assumed that the different tactile submodalities are segregated at least through primary somatosensory cortex (Sur et al., 1981; Sur et al., 1984; Chen et al., 2001; Friedman et al., 2004) (although cortical PC neurons have generally proven elusive, see below), recent evidence suggests that input from different classes of somatosensory afferents is indeed integrated between periphery and cortex (Saal and Bensmaia, 2014; Pei et al., 2009; Carter et al., 2014; Prescott et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: SA1 and RA input have been shown to be integrated in the responses of S1 neurons when studied with ramp-and-hold skin indentations.
source: However, SA1 and RA input have been shown to be integrated in the responses of S1 neurons when these were studied with ramp-and-hold skin indentations (Pei et al., 2009) so the convergence of submodality-specific input onto individual S1 neurons seems to be a general phenomenon.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Convergence of somatosensory submodalities has been observed in the brainstem of rats.
source: Convergence of somatosensory submodalities has been observed in the brainstem of rats (Sakurai et al., 2013) and the same is likely true in primates.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work in rats.

claim: Vibrotactile coding and the role of PC input have been probed almost exclusively with high-frequency sinusoidal stimuli.
source: First, vibrotactile coding in general and the role of PC input specifically have been probed almost exclusively with high-frequency sinusoidal stimuli.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical approach in the field, drawing from general knowledge.

claim: High-frequency sinusoidal stimuli evoke only a short transient response in S1, which then quickly decays back to baseline.
source: These stimuli have been shown to evoke only a short transient response in S1, which then quickly decays back to baseline, a phenomenon that can be accounted for by the balance of excitation and suppression in the PC drive.
evidence: This claim draws from established observations and is explained by the current findings.

claim: PC-driven cortical neurons are thought to be extremely rare in S1.
source: That PC-elicited responses are short and weak might explain why PC-driven cortical neurons are thought to be extremely rare in S1 (Lebedev and Nelson, 1996; Mountcastle et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is offered as an explanation based on the current findings.

claim: The extremely precise timing of S1 responses at high frequencies contributes to tactile perception.
source: Second, the main effect of PC input is to shape the timing of cortical spikes, which could account for the extremely precise timing of S1 responses at high frequencies (Harvey et al., 2013) that has been shown to contribute to tactile perception (Zuo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The balanced drive of PC afferents explains why the firing rates of S1 neurons are not dependent on stimulus frequency even though PC rates are.
source: Third, the balanced drive of PC afferents explains why the firing rates of S1 neurons are not dependent on stimulus frequency even though PC rates are (Harvey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an explanation based on the current findings and a citation to prior work.

claim: PC input has been found to inhibit cortical responses.
source: Finally, the PC input has been found to inhibit cortical responses (Tommerdahl et al., 2005; Tommerdahl et al., 2010), consistent with our finding that PC filters are often net suppressive.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is consistent with the current findings.

claim: Sensory cortex is tuned to the statistics of the natural environment.
source: Sensory cortex is tuned to the statistics of the natural environment, as has been demonstrated most notably in vision (van Hateren, 1992; Field, 1987) and audition (Smith and Lewicki, 2006), by invoking the efficient coding principle (Barlow et al., 1961).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in vision and audition.

claim: RA afferents increase their firing rate with increasing stimulus amplitudes in a manner that is relatively independent of stimulus frequency.
source: First, RA afferents increase their firing rate with increasing stimulus amplitudes (Arabzadeh et al., 2014), and do so in a manner that is relatively independent of stimulus frequency, while PC responses saturate at low stimulus amplitudes and are highly frequency-dependent (Muniak et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PC responses saturate at low stimulus amplitudes and are highly frequency-dependent.
source: First, RA afferents increase their firing rate with increasing stimulus amplitudes (Arabzadeh et al., 2014), and do so in a manner that is relatively independent of stimulus frequency, while PC responses saturate at low stimulus amplitudes and are highly frequency-dependent (Muniak et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RA firing rates convey a more informative signal about the amplitude of tactile stimuli than do PC firing rates.
source: RA firing rates therefore convey a much more informative signal about the amplitude of tactile stimuli than do PC firing rates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the different response properties of RA and PC afferents.

claim: PC afferents exhibit much higher temporal precision in their spiking patterns than do RA afferents.
source: Second, PC afferents exhibit much higher temporal precision in their spiking patterns than do RA afferents (Mackevicius et al., 2012), especially for high-frequency skin vibrations such as those elicited when we run our fingers across a texture (Weber et al., 2013), and this precise spike timing conveys information about tactile events and shapes perception (Mackevicius et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PC precise spike timing conveys information about tactile events and shapes perception.
source: Second, PC afferents exhibit much higher temporal precision in their spiking patterns than do RA afferents (Mackevicius et al., 2012), especially for high-frequency skin vibrations such as those elicited when we run our fingers across a texture (Weber et al., 2013), and this precise spike timing conveys information about tactile events and shapes perception (Mackevicius et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Separate sensory channels that convey complementary but overlapping information are commonplace in sensory systems.
source: Separate sensory channels that convey complementary but overlapping information are commonplace in sensory systems and not limited to the sense of touch; the visual (Field and Chichilnisky, 2007), auditory (Cant and Benson, 2003), gustatory (Zhang et al., 2003), olfactory (Uchida et al., 2014), and vestibular (Goldberg, 2000; Sadeghi et al., 2007) systems all involve many types of afferents.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work across multiple sensory modalities.

claim: Distributing sensory information across channels has distinct advantages such as parsing the behaviorally relevant range, keeping energy expenditure low, and optimizing information transmission in the presence of noise.
source: Distributing sensory information across channels has distinct advantages such as parsing the behaviorally relevant range (Dominy and Lucas, 2001), keeping energy expenditure low (Gjorgjieva et al., 2014), and optimizing information transmission in the presence of noise (Kastner et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Tactile stimuli were delivered to the distal pads of the digits using a stainless steel probe driven by a shaker motor.
source: In short, tactile stimuli were delivered to the distal pads of the digits using a stainless steel probe diameter driven by a shaker motor.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Three types of stimuli were delivered: simple sinusoids, diharmonic stimuli, and bandpass noise.
source: We delivered three types of stimuli that varied in spectral complexity, including simple sinusoids, diharmonic stimuli (only used for the peripheral model fitting), and bandpass noise.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Individual stimuli were 1 s long and were repeated five times.
source: Individual stimuli in this data set were 1 s long and were repeated five times (frozen noise), yielding a total of about 22 minutes (16 for noise and 6 for the sinusoids) of data from each neuron.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Extracellular recordings were made in the postcentral gyri in four hemispheres of two awake, behaving Rhesus macaques.
source: Extracellular recordings were made in the postcentral gyri in four hemispheres of two awake, behaving Rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Single unit recordings were made from the ulnar and median nerves of two anesthetized Rhesus macaques.
source: Single unit recordings were made from the ulnar and median nerves of two anesthetized Rhesus macaques using standard methods (Talbot et al., 1968).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Integrate-and-fire models were fit to the measured responses of individual afferents.
source: We fit integrate-and-fire (IF) models to the measured responses of individual afferents.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling methods.

claim: The peripheral models captured both the strength and timing of peripheral afferents.
source: The models have been extensively validated, as detailed in previous studies (Kim et al., 2010; Dong et al., 2013), and captured both the strength and timing of peripheral afferents (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior validation work and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The transformation between peripheral RA and PC population responses and single unit S1 responses was modeled using the LNP framework.
source: We modeled the transformation between the peripheral RA and PC population responses and single unit S1 responses using the LNP framework (Schwartz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach with a citation.

claim: LNP models have been fruitfully used for modeling the responses of cortical neurons across several synapses.
source: LNP models have long been fruitfully used for modeling the responses of cortical neurons across several synapses, often even including the sensory receptors.
evidence: This is a statement about the established use of LNP models in neuroscience.

claim: Textured surfaces were scanned over the fingertip of human subjects at different scanning speeds while elicited vibrations were recorded using a Laser Doppler vibrometer.
source: In brief, textured surfaces were scanned over the fingertip of human subjects at different scanning speeds, while elicited vibrations were recorded using a Laser Doppler vibrometer (Polytec OFV-3001 with OFV 311 sensor head, Polytec, Inc., Irvine, CA).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods for texture scanning.

claim: For each texture, 240 (8 subjects × 3 speeds × 10 repetitions) 500-ms long vibration traces were collected.
source: For each texture, we collected 240 (8 subjects × 3 speeds × 10 repetitions) 500-ms long vibration traces.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collection.

claim: Across textures, the recorded and simulated firing rates matched well (r = 0.83 for RA and r = 0.92 for PC responses).
source: Indeed, across textures the recorded and simulated firing rates matched well (r = 0.83 for RA and r = 0.92 for PC responses), indicating that our simulated responses capture actual texture-elicited responses well.
evidence: This is a quantitative result validating the peripheral models for texture responses.

claim: Linear filters were optimized for each texture individually by maximizing the mutual information between the model responses and the texture-elicited vibration traces.
source: Next, we optimized linear filters for each texture individually by maximizing the mutual information I(S,V) between the responses of our model (S) and the texture-elicited vibration traces (V):
evidence: This is a description of the optimization procedure.

claim: Most frequency-amplitude pairs elicit responses from both RA and PC afferent classes.
source: While RA and PC afferents are maximally sensitive at different frequencies, most frequency–amplitude pairs elicit responses from both afferent classes (indicated by the shaded region).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1A showing the overlapping response regions.

claim: The model predictions closely approximate measured peripheral firing rates for sinusoidal vibrations.
source: Recorded (top) and simulated (bottom) responses of RA and PC populations to sinusoidal skin vibrations of different amplitude and frequency. The model predictions closely approximate measured firing rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both recorded and modeled PC afferents exhibit entrainment plateaus.
source: Rate-intensity function for a recorded (top) and simulated (bottom) PC afferent stimulated with 200 Hz sinusoidal vibrations. Both the recorded and modeled PC afferent exhibit entrainment plateaus.
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At low amplitudes, PC afferents produce a single spike per cycle that is precisely timed to occur at the same phase within the cycle.
source: At low amplitudes, a single spike is elicited per cycle, which is precisely timed to occur at the same phase within the cycle (left column).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: At higher amplitudes, PC afferents can produce more than one spike per cycle in complex but repeatable patterns.
source: At higher amplitudes, more than one spike per cycle can occur in complex but repeatable patterns (right column) (Whitsel et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and a citation.

claim: The simulated spike train matches the recorded ones with high temporal precision for bandpass noise stimuli.
source: Recorded (black) and simulated (lavender) response a single PC fiber to stimulus. The simulated spike train matches the recorded ones with high temporal precision.
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The lower correlation for RA responses at the finest temporal resolution reflects the fact that RA responses are not very repeatable at those timescales.
source: The lower correlation for the RA responses at the finest temporal resolution reflects the fact that RA responses are not very repeatable at those timescales (Mackevicius et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and a citation.

claim: The spike triggered averages for the model and the recorded peripheral data agree well.
source: The STA for the model and the recorded peripheral data agree well.
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Due to jitter in the recorded spike trains, the predictable variance decreases for finer bin sizes.
source: Due to jitter in the recorded spike trains, the predictable variance decreases for finer bin sizes.
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Cortical neurons differ in their response properties, such as burstiness and temporal precision.
source: Cortical neurons differ in their response properties, such as burstiness and temporal precision, and the model captures these broad differences with different RA and PC filters.
evidence: This is evident from Figure 1E showing different neurons with different filter shapes.

claim: The model captures broad differences in cortical neuron response properties with different RA and PC filters.
source: Cortical neurons differ in their response properties, such as burstiness and temporal precision, and the model captures these broad differences with different RA and PC filters.
evidence: This is evident from Figure 1E showing model predictions matching different neuron types.

claim: The magnitude of PC filters was correlated with that of RA filters (r = 0.41).
source: First, while the magnitude of the PC filters was correlated with that of the RA filters (r = 0.41), PC filters were consistently of lower magnitude (Figure 2C, t(70) = 6.4, p < 0.01, paired t-test), with the RA contribution on average about three times stronger than the PC one.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the filter analysis.

claim: PC filters were much more diverse than RA filters and spanned the range of excitation/suppression indices from -1 to +1.
source: PC filters were also much more diverse and spanned the range of this metric (from -1 to +1), in contrast to RA filters, which, as mentioned above, tended to be net excitatory (>0).
evidence: This is evident from Figure 2E showing the distribution of excitation indices.

claim: RA filters tended to be net excitatory (>0).
source: PC filters were also much more diverse and spanned the range of this metric (from -1 to +1), in contrast to RA filters, which, as mentioned above, tended to be net excitatory (>0).
evidence: This is evident from the excitation index analysis.

claim: The balanced drive of PC afferents can account for the short transient response in S1 to high-frequency sinusoidal stimuli.
source: These stimuli have been shown to evoke only a short transient response in S1, which then quickly decays back to baseline, a phenomenon that can be accounted for by the balance of excitation and suppression in the PC drive.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the balanced PC filters to observed cortical response properties.

claim: The integration of parallel input channels should reflect and exploit differences in their response properties.
source: To the extent that these parallel input channels represent information in disparate ways (differing in response latency, adaptation properties, or spiking precision, among others), their integration should reflect and exploit such differences, a process that can be described using the type of model introduced here.
evidence: This is a general principle inferred from the findings and applicable to sensory systems broadly.
